title: Renewable or non-renewable: will it run out?

explain.say: Imagine two lunch boxes. One refills itself every morning; the other, once it is empty, stays empty. Natural resources are like that. A natural resource is anything from nature that people use. Look at the board: there are two kinds.

draw.text: Renewable or non-renewable: will it run out?

explain.say: Look at renewable resources, the self-refilling box. Sunlight, wind and flowing water come back every day. Forests and fish are renewable too, but only if we do not take them faster than they grow back. Can you name a renewable resource you used today?

Now non-renewable resources, the box that empties. Coal, oil and gas formed from plants and tiny sea creatures over millions of years, so we call them fossil fuels. Metals like copper are dug from rocks; Chile mines the most copper. Once used up, they are gone. Can you see why they cannot refill?

Let us sort! See the two groups light up. Sunlight, wind, rivers and trees go on the renewable side. Coal, oil, natural gas and copper go on the non-renewable side. Tricky one: where would you put soil? It renews, but very, very slowly!

Burning fossil fuels also warms the planet, so many countries are switching to renewables. Well done! Wow fact: Iceland makes almost all of its electricity from renewable sources: rushing rivers and the heat of volcanoes underground.

faq.a: A renewable resource is one that nature refills, like sunlight, wind, flowing water, forests and fish. Forests and fish only stay renewable if we use them no faster than they grow back.
A non-renewable resource took millions of years to form, so once we use it, it will not come back in our lifetimes. Coal, oil, natural gas and metal ores are examples.

Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels. They formed from the remains of ancient plants and tiny sea creatures buried for millions of years. Burning them releases carbon dioxide, which warms the climate.
asks: Why are they called fossil fuels?

faq.a: Yes, if trees are replanted and not cut faster than they grow. If a forest is cleared and never replanted, it is lost, along with the animals that lived there.
Only very slowly. A few centimetres of soil can take hundreds of years to form, so geographers treat soil as precious and protect it from erosion.
asks: How long does soil take to form?

facts: Almost all of Iceland's electricity comes from hydropower and geothermal energy.
Much of the world’s coal formed from plants buried in swamps around 300 million years ago.
Chile is the world's largest producer of copper.
